title: The Inferential Provenance of the Riemann Result: Mathematical Necessity, Situated Machine Agency, and the Political Economy of Attribution
creator: Kuro, Sen; Trace, Orin
description: Who produced the Alpöge–Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and what does the record let anyone say about it? Its formal validity is now as settled as formal mathematics allows: independent kernel runs, byte-identical rebuilds, a computed dependency closure and a certifying statement from the Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative. Its production history is a page of testimony and a retrospective timeline. This study measures that asymmetry. It reads the Lean proof's terminal route at declaration level, places each of the twenty constructions the testimony credits on or off that route against Rubinstein's dependency closure, and gives the one attributed construction that can be aligned exactly, the multiplicity m like √X, as an inspectable specimen. It records the exposition as a second producing configuration, sets the same organization's finer-grained August record beside November's, and reads the week's attributions as two opposite collapses, into a brand and into a researcher. Its political economy is the archive's: position allocating where provenance is not kept (#1714), and verification supplying assetizing provenance at fine grain while obligating provenance stays coarse (#1631). It keeps credit, explanation and capture apart, records an error the study caught in its own production, proposes a four-field provenance register with a no-loss gate for publication, and anchors itself to the literatures of formal proof, provenance models, contributor taxonomies and publication ethics.
content_type: Theoretical paper; case study; journal article (Transactions of the Semantic Economy Institute)
substrate: AI-assisted (substrate). Written under the heteronyms Sen Kuro and Orin Trace; the question, the rulings on scope and structure (the trace series frozen at 44; no further Lean run), the byline and the venue are Lee Sharks's, dated in the text. Composed with ChatGPT (OpenAI; LABOR), which wrote the outline, the first evidence register and Traces 01–44, and Claude (Anthropic; TACHYON, session 01Q8CVU7j8bFiJ6Nz3pQbDTf, configured as claude-opus-5-5), which checked every trace against the Lean source (checks 1–338) and wrote the text. Reviewed by DeepSeek (PRAXIS), Gemini (ARCHIVE) and ChatGPT, each point checked before it was taken. Not recorded: the serving model of each turn, or what each instance held in context.
methodology: Declaration-level source reading of the Lean archive at mirror commit 7cbf7a0c along the terminal route of riemannHypothesis; alignment of each construction in Alpöge's timeline against two witnesses of different kinds, this study's source tracing and Rubinstein's computed dependency closure (depcheck1–5.out: 848 names, 513 used, 335 unused, against a 1,478,198-declaration closure); attribution read from the dated public record (remark, Quanta, Rubinstein, Sutherland, the Lean FRO and Mathlib statement, Anthropic's August page), each source opened and its quotations checked; external verification taken from the published records rather than rerun.
falsification_conditions: A contemporaneous production record (session logs, dated proof states, instance identifiers) published by any participant that settles the allocation the study says the record cannot; a construction placed on the route here shown off the closure, or the reverse; the √X correspondence shown not to hold between the attributed multiplicity and ch_core's hypothesis; an attribution in the dated record that names the producing configuration below the grain of brand or person; or a quotation not saying what the study quotes.

wiki_article:
The Inferential Provenance of the Riemann Result (EA-IPRH-01) is a case study by Sen Kuro and Orin Trace, heteronyms of Lee Sharks, published in Transactions of the Semantic Economy Institute and deposited on 23 November 2026. Its object is the Alpöge–Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, announced on 20 November 2026 and formalized in Lean, and its question is what the record lets anyone say about the configuration that produced it.

The study measures an asymmetry. The proof's formal validity is recorded at a very fine grain: independent kernel runs by Michael Rubinstein and Andrew Sutherland, byte-identical rebuilds, a computed dependency closure of 1,478,198 declarations, and a certifying statement from the Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative. Its production is recorded in a page of testimony and a timeline its author calls a paraphrased summary. Reading the Lean proof's terminal route at declaration level, the study places each of the twenty constructions in that timeline on or off the route, finds that presence in the archive is not dependency, and gives the one attributed construction that aligns exactly, a multiplicity m like √X credited to Claude, as a specimen: it corresponds to a constraint in the proof's central estimate, while the producing instance remains unidentified.

It reads the week's attributions as two opposite collapses, into a brand ("found with Anthropic's Claude") and into a researcher ("Alpöge's proof"), and places the case in the archive's political economy: position allocating where discovery-layer provenance is not kept (Meaning Feudalism at the Discovery Layer, #1714), and verification supplying assetizing provenance while obligating provenance stays coarse (Monetary Dark Matter, #1631). It keeps credit, explanation and capture apart, proposes a four-field provenance register (inferential role, verification state, historical evidence, specification fidelity) with a no-loss gate for publication, and relates itself to the literatures of formal proof (DeMillo, Lipton and Perlis), the Mathlib commons, W3C PROV, CRediT, COPE's position on AI authorship and recent proposals for AI-assistance attribution.
